text: Huh, ice always floats. So why doesn't that happen with other stuff?
When water freezes, its molecules lock into a six-sided pattern - and that actually spreads them further apart.
So the same weight of ice ends up taking up more space.
That's called density - how much space something takes up for its weight. Ice has lower density, so it floats.
This expanding force is actually strong enough to burst frozen water pipes in winter.
Since ice is lighter than water, when a lake freezes, only the surface freezes - the water underneath stays liquid. That's how fish survive the winter, right below the ice.
There's also a claim that under the right conditions, hot water can freeze before cold water. It's called the Mpemba effect, and people still argue about why.
